utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Please be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the interpreters. I see that they're all there. Good morning to the technical booth, the court reporters, everybody in the courtroom, the accused. I see that the Defence counsels are all there, the Prosecution, the witness. Have you had a good rest, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're going to continue answering the questions that Mr. Keegan is going to ask you. And without further ado, I give the floor to Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, yesterday at the recess, you were speaking generally of some of the conditions in the camp. I'd like to continue along that line. While you were in the camp, did you have the opportunity or were you at any time placed inside the large building that you identified earlier as the hangar?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And were you placed in the area that we might call the main area, the ground-floor area of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During the time that that facility was being used as the camp, were prisoners housed on the entire area of that ground floor? In other words, did they use the entire area of the ground floor as an area to hold prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Approximately how much of that ground-floor area did they use to house prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 60 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what was in the other approximately 40 per cent of that ground-floor area?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were large trucks which we referred to as the dumpers to convey mine and ore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If that equipment had been moved out of that ground-floor area of the hangar, would there have been sufficient room to allow the prisoners on the pista to move in from the outside?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost, yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the camp and in the hangar building, were the materials in there from which bedding for the prisoners, for example, could have been fashioned?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there material or equipment available within the facilities, the buildings of that camp, from which latrines could have been constructed on the outside for the prisoners to use?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If all the parts and possibilities were used of the different equipment, the machines or anything else, then probably they could be used to make things of that kind, latrines or something similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there tractors, construction equipment available from which trenches could have been dug?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there pieces of wood, rails, and metal rails available from which such things could have been constructed?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We usually used only the cartons of boxes or different shapes of paper, paper in different shapes that we would place on the pista, and that was a sort of surface mat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes. My question was referring to material available from which proper latrines could have been built, such as pieces of wood or metal rails, things like that.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So that equipment, that material was not available?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could using the taps, which you identified water taps outside that were available, could washing of clothes and personal hygiene have been organised amongst the prisoners to achieve better personal hygiene?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except for the last week before the camp was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: My question was: Could it have been organised, not was it. Could it have been organised?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why couldn't it have been organised?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we weren't permitted things like that and because there weren't enough taps or latrines, toilets, or detergents which we could use for that purpose, for all the things you enumerated, for washing, for shaving, or anything of that sort, the washing of clothes or cleaning in general, footwear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the Omarska camp, was some of your family members still in the town of Prijedor? Were some of your family members -- excuse me -- still in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If it had been permitted, would they have been in a position to send you extra clothing, soap, things like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I object to that question. He's asking the witness to speculate on something that appears to be beyond the scope of this witness's knowledge. It's hard to imagine how he would know what would be going on in the town of Prijedor in he was in Omarska. He's asking the witness to speculate, and I submit that that's an inappropriate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan, what is your response to the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness to take off his headphones and perhaps determine whether he understands the language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, Mr. O'Sullivan. Have you finished or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The procedure we've been following is we ask the witness to remove his headphones and, first of all, to establish whether he understands English or French, because this debate should not be going on in front of the witness. We're going to be discussing where we're headed with this, and we -- it's not fair for the witness to be understanding what we're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you take your headphones off, please? Do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat. Do you understand English, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you take your headset off, please. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's the only point I wanted to add to my objection was the question of whether or not the witness could understand and hear us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would be happy to go through the foundational questions to indicate that the witness met up with his family after his release of the camp, was aware of their circumstances while he was in Prijedor, and then could testify that yes, in fact, they would have been in the position to send things had it been permitted. I was merely short-cutting those foundation questions based on the fact that he knew they were in Prijedor and presumably that obviously he'd be in a position to know. I'm happy to go through those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Perhaps you could reformulate your question, Mr. Keegan, if you would. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, when you were released from the Omarska camp, which camp were you sent to?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And upon your release from Trnopolje, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned home to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And who was at your family home in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father, my mother, my wife, and my child. At the time I had one child, a son.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How long had they been in the family home since the 30th of May? Had they been there the entire time?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire time, until my return on the 14th of August, 1992, and a month and a half to two months after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were the majority of your clothes still in your family home after you were arrested on 30 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether your family had soap and other hygiene materials in the family home during the period you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they have food, some amount of food to eat during the time you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, to go back to my earlier question, in your opinion, if it had been permitted, would your family have been in a position to send you personal hygiene material such as soap and extra clothing to you in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must object again. He's asking him to give an opinion without any basis for asking that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think and I wish to say that in this case, Mr. Keegan can continue with the question. It is important, from the point of view of the matter we're discussing here, that is to say, to know whether there were possibilities of changing the conditions. So we reject your objection, and we're going to ask Mr. Keegan to continue.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could have sent them had there been the possibility of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, were prisoners beaten in the Omarska camp during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In what types of situations would beatings occur?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions. Under number 1, when the prisoners were taken to the upper floor of the main building or the central building for interrogation; number 2, when we went to lunch; number 3, when we went to the WC or to fetch water; and under number 4, during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What would happen during the evenings, during the night?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Terrible screams could be heard, moans, beatings, from practically all the rooms which served as the Omarska concentration camp. Mostly in the hangar, the canteen, the pista, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you see the physical indications of these beatings that you've talked about? Could you see injuries or marks on prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe that, what some of those injuries looked like.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the many times that I went to lunch, that is to say, once in the course of the day, every day, you could see enormous differences or changes amongst the detainees. Most of the differences or changes occurred with the detainees in the "white house," who, when they went to lunch, had injuries all over their head, all over their body. They had injuries to their back; they had bruises. They had scabs on their ears, on their head. Their hands would be bandaged in any T-shirts or whatever clothing they had, makeshift bandages, and so forth. When they went to be questioned, or when we went to be questioned rather, the people who questioned us, the interrogators, in the central building also, you could see similar or so-called self-injury. In the course of going to interrogation and the return journey from the interrogation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: -- the guards were beaten, the witness said.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Not the guards, I meant the prisoners, they were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, yesterday you spoke of the problems of dysentery and other illnesses, the food, the type of food that the prisoners received, the problem with the toilets and access to water, and this morning, the beatings. As a result of all of these conditions, what was the condition of the prisoners in the Omarska camp? What did they look like by the time that the month of July came to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was hardly a prisoner who had not lost at least 20 kilograms or so. I personally lost 18 kilograms in weight. As for the prisoners who were in the hangar, inside the hangar, there was a terrible stench, stink. I don't know how to describe this smell. The smell was like that of dead animals because they didn't have many opportunities to go outside; in fact, only once a day when they went for lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did the clothing of the prisoners look like by July?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some prisoners hardly had anything left on them. It was torn, it was in rags, it was dirty. I had high shoes, which were almost new before I went to the camp. From urine, going to the toilet, and the stink, and the fact that I had to relieve myself so often, those shoes were virtually destroyed. This applies to the prisoners' other footwear, because all we had was what we came in, whether it was on the 30th or the 31st of May, or in June. So those were the clothes that we had on us, and the footwear as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What about the prisoners' hair and their facial hair?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our hair had grown; it was dirty. Some people cut their hair themselves. They managed to hide so that others wouldn't see. Facial hair had grown, moustaches, beards. We had lice. As we sat next to one another, we could see visibly the lice crawling over people's hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did any officials visit the Omarska camp from the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When was that visit?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July. I can't tell you the exact date but somewhere around then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were the prisoners required to do anything for that visit?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three days prior to the visit, special preparations were carried out so that we would be ready to welcome the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were those special preparations?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all taken out to sit on the pista, in front of the central building, in front of the hangar, and we sang "Boze Pravde," which means God and Justice; "Ko To Kaze, Ko To Laze" [Translation: Who is Saying, Who is Lying]. We had to applaud Serbia. We had to lift our hands, with the three fingers pointed in the Serb manner, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Those two songs that you mentioned, what kind of songs are those?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chetnik nationalist songs. Those songs were sung during the Second World War, during the Chetnik movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the condition of the prisoners at the time of this visit? What did they look like?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exhausted, sitting there and having to do what I have just said, humiliated. I have no words to describe the feeling, the humiliation. It was perhaps the worst thing that could have happened to me in the camp. Degrading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were the prisoners in the physical condition that you've earlier described at the time of this visit?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were in a poor physical and mental condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You mentioned, among the other things the prisoners were required to do when the delegation visited, that you had to lift your hands, with the three fingers pointed in the Serb manner. Can you demonstrate for the Judges what that was and explain the significance of that.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. First of all, I thought I shouldn't show you, but in the interests of the investigation I will do so probably for the last time in my life. It was like this [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What is the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. I wasn't interested. It was a Serb sign. I really never investigated or inquired what it meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people who were in the delegation that visited the camp in July, those officials?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. It was a mixed delegation from Banja Luka and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who, among the delegation, did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anyone from Banja Luka personally. But a day or two prior to the visit, the guards were talking amongst themselves and one of them was somebody called Brk Tadic, who was the right-hand man of Mr. Meakic, and he prepared us for this, he said that Vukic, Radic [Realtime transcript read in error "Mladic"], Kupresanin, Brdjanin were coming. Whether they all came, I don't know, but that was the composition of the delegation, and some others whose names I cannot remember from Banja Luka. As from Prijedor, there was Simo Miskovic, Simo Drljaca, Slobodan Kuruzovic, all the investigators who interrogated people in the Omarska concentration camp, the commanders and deputy commanders of the camp, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, during the time that you were in the Omarska camp, did you witness any shootings?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, how many shootings did you witness?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, you have something to tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I just wish to point out that the name that is entered in the transcript was "Mladic"; it should be Radic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is apologising.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not the witness' fault. It was just an error in the transcript. It should be Radic and not Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I myself heard Radic. I see "Mladic" in the transcript. Thank you very much, Mr. Fila, for drawing our attention to this. Mr. Keegan, could you perhaps check with the witness again so that we can correct it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, you heard the point raised by Mr. Fila. Can you confirm the last name of the person. Was it Mladic or Radic?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radic. Radic. I apologise if I made a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you describe, please, the first shooting that you witnessed.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first shooting of which I was an eyewitness occurred a week, or maybe ten days after my arrival in the Omarska concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where did that shooting take place?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the central building, in the canteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What time of day was it that this shooting occurred?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusk, nightfall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why were you in the canteen at that time?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that is where we would spend the night in the beginning, those of us who were at the pista during the daytime, to make it quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you please describe what happened.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the canteen, when we went to sleep there, there was always about 600 people. I will explain how I know the figure. There were 20 groups of 30 men, which makes a total of 600, which means that we couldn't sit, never mind lie down, it was so crowded. Suddenly, during that night, or early in the night -- we were not allowed to get up; we had to raise our hand and ask the guard if we could go to the toilet, and only when given permission we could go -- a man got up. I know that his surname is Nasic; I think his first name was Mehmedalija. I'm not sure. And he started muttering something. Obviously something was wrong. He was saying, "What are you doing to us? Long live brotherhood and unity. We've all lived well together." He even mentioned Tito. I saw that something must be wrong with his mental condition. Then the closest guard to us was Milan Pavlic, who warned him once and told him to sit down. A second time he cautioned him. However, Nasic didn't hear, or he wasn't conscious of what was going on, I can't judge. And the third time, Pavlic opened fire at him, and, in fact, he was aiming at all of us because this burst of fire could not hit just Nasic but also the people around him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where was the victim Nasic at the time he was shot?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the canteen there is a line or a belt along which we walked when we went to have lunch, and only two or three metres from the large glass window, so in that part of the canteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where was the guard Pavlic?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three metres from the large glass window of the canteen, or one of the large glass windows of the canteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was he inside the canteen or outside the canteen?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside? You mean the guard?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the canteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The guard Pavlic was physically outside of the building.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When he fired, did he fire through the glass window?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After the shooting, did you see any of the camp command staff present?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the commander of the camp, Zeljko Meakic, and his assistant Kvocka, and the whole shift, led by Krkan, because Milan Pavlic belonged to Krkan's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened with Nasic, and were there any other people who were hit by the bullets?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nasic passed away very quickly. He was carried out to the grass, the part of the pista next to the grass, and three other persons were wounded. I know them very well, but I won't mention them now, who were taken to Banja Luka. We didn't know at the time where they were taken. After about a month, they were brought back from Banja Luka. They were taken to the hospital in Banja Luka, and they came back, and they were not allowed to have contact with anyone once they returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, did any of the camp command staff that you've identified say anything to the prisoners that evening after the shooting, that you recall?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was first confusion amongst themselves. I think they themselves didn't expect that to happen, with the exception of Milan Pavlic, who was drunk, I must add. A lot of confusion and disturbance occurred, because they realised that a lot of people had witnessed the event. Later on, Zeljko Meakic, the commander of the camp arrived, and angrily and arrogantly he addressed all of us and said that that would happen to everyone who tries to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the other shooting that you yourself witnessed while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A shooting that occurred shortly after the killing of Nasic and the wounding of the other three persons. I'm sorry for this sigh, because it was a very moving event for all of us who witnessed it. It happened in Bijela Kuca, the killing of Becir Medjunjanin, and a young boy called Hankin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could move on from that shooting, and we'll describe that event later. Can you describe the next shooting that you witnessed in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next shooting was a shooting that occurred also after the return of prisoners from lunch. On that day, a group of prisoners was coming back from lunch, which was served in the largest premises of the central building, which later came to be known as Mujo's room. We would usually, on the way back from lunch, have to run, as the path from the canteen to the main room in the central building is not a long one. A group of some 30 prisoners, and we always ate in groups of 30, was running back to this central building and the main room in it. Then one of those prisoners, a man in his 60s, a well-known fire brigade member and fisherman nicknamed Hadzo -- he lived in my neighbourhood, close to me -- suddenly deviated from the path. And instead of entering the room where he had been staying until then, he started running towards the exit of the camp, towards the village of Omarska itself. That very same moment, we heard a burst of fire that hit Hadzo. Hadzo was wounded, but he survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see who fired at Hadzo?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Soskan, a guard nicknamed Soskan. I don't know his real name, but I'm convinced it was he. That was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you know whose shift this guard Soskan worked on?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And which shift was that?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krkan's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, did you know a man named Safet Ramadanovic?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nicknamed Cifut? Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was he a prisoner in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you aware of any incidents in which he was involved?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Would you please describe what incidents you saw.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Safet Ramadanovic, Cifut, was a well-known caterer in Prijedor. He was the owner of a cafe called Rudar in the centre of town. He was married. He had two children; two daughters. He was my neighbour. Safet Ramadanovic, Cifut, came later to the Omarska concentration camp, and I will explain what I mean later, which means he didn't come when most of us came on the 30th and 31st of May. Every day, five or six new prisoners would be brought in in a police car which we called the Marica. Upon his very arrival at the concentration camp, Saft Ramadanovic, Cifut, was beaten. And, anyway, that was customary. The new prisoners were first beaten and then assigned to various rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, did you see that beating that Mr. Ramadanovic received on his arrival?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see who beat Mr. Ramadanovic?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And do you know their name?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Popovic, also known as Pop; Zeljko Savic; Drazenko Predojevic; a guard called Zoka; a guard with the surname Kricka; and many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you know what shift those guards worked on?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krkan's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Ramadanovic after that beating?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ramadanovic was taken to the central building, the largest premises in that building, to join the other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened when you saw Mr. Ramadanovic next?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a week -- I'm not sure how long -- Mr. Ramadanovic was taken in for interrogation, because everyone had to go through this procedure. Some people once, other people, two, three, or four times. As he was waiting for the interrogation, at the very entrance to the central building, the guards or, rather, the prisoners had to wait, and sometimes, not always, I must admit, they were beaten. And on that day, when Safet Ramadanovic, Cifut, went for interrogation, he was waiting and was beaten again, which means a second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see that beating yourself?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see who was beating Ramadanovic?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same group of guards that beat him the first time, Popovic called Pop; Drazenko Predorjevic; Savic; Zoka; Kricka; and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And once again, whose shift did they work on?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krkan's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened after that beating outside the administration building?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Safet Ramadanovic, Cifut, was taken upstairs. He was interrogated and beaten. Two prisoners carried him down because he couldn't come down alone -- these two were with me on the pista -- and they lay him down on a part of the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You stated he was interrogated and beaten. How do you know that he was beaten while he was upstairs being interrogated?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he came back in a much worse condition than he was when he went up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After he was placed on the pista, what happened?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken away again; that is to say, individual prisoners secretly took him into the room where he had been until then, that is, the main central building, at the bottom of the main central building, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see him again that day?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken out dead and laid on the grass next to the canteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At the time he was taken out of the room in the administration building, how can you be sure that he was dead?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before he died, he breathed with great difficulty. He was almost not able to walk. He had been carried by two men, and they took care of him after that event. They were two brothers. And later on, when they took him out, you couldn't hear a sound from him, and they carried him like a bag of sand. You know that a bag of sand is like a dead body. It gives no signs of life. And like a bag of sand, they placed him down, as I said, on the grass next to the pista, near the canteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see the body, where they put it down on the grass, from where you were sitting on the pista?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did Safet Ramadanovic move at all once they put him on the grass?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he make any sound?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How long was his body out there on the grass?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. Between two to four hours. Two to three hours, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what happened to his body?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, his son came to the camp, who was a Serb, and he was married to one of -- his son-in-law, actually. He was married to one of his two daughters; that is to say, his son-in-law. I think I said "son" a moment ago. And he was married to one of the daughters of Safet, Cifut, and his name was Miso, and I knew him well. And he came up to the body of Safet, Cifut.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see the body actually taken away?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I just saw Miso standing by the body of Safet Cifut.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, did you known a man named Rizah Hadzalic?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Rizo Hadzalic is the name, because I know him well. If there is an error in the writing of his name, he was Rizo Hadzalic, nicknamed Rizah, and he was my neighbour in Muharem Suljanovic Street, in the same street and house which carried the plaque of a former hero. Later on, he got an apartment at the Pecani settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was he a prisoner in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came later on from the Keraterm concentration camp, as I already described. It was one of these daily new arrivals of five or six prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see an incident that involved Rizo Hadzalic?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And could you describe that, please?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rizo Hadzalic came from Keraterm, and as he was a person who liked to laugh a lot, a witty whom we all knew, he didn't know what was actually going on in the Omarska camp. On that particular day, when he was taken out on to the pista, that is to say, for interrogation, from that main central building, the biggest one, Mujo's, known as Mujo's room, he had to wait up against one of the walls at the very entrance to the main central building, with his head and face turned towards the wall and his hands up behind his head. At that time, and it was around 11.00 a.m. or 12.00 a.m., and I know that because we usually had a snack at that time, we referred to it as Marenda, and these guards would go out for a midday snack, for a sandwich, salami, ham, or whatever, and they ate. And they would always have a good meal, and they always showed how delicious their meal was, because they knew we were hungry, so they cluck their lips and so on, and they would talk to each other, the guards, amongst themselves. At that moment, Rizo Hadzalic, nicknamed Rizah, said a word which is very well known and which was used by the Muslims and Serbs in Bosnia. The word was -- and when you eat, if you want to invite someone to join you, we say "bujrum," and that word means, in translation,"Please go ahead. Would you like to join us? Would you like something to eat?" At that particular moment, when he said that particular word, there was hell. All hell broke loose. The guards cursed his Muslim and Turkish mother and said, "You saying bujrum to us in this place," and they began beating him with everything they had. When I say "everything they had," let me explain what that means; with their clubs and batons, with their rifles, with their automatic rifles. They kicked him with their legs, with their arms, everything. They used everything they could to beat him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see the guards who were beating Rizah Hadzalic?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that particular moment, we were ordered to lie down on the pista with our hands bowed down facing the pista. But we always used one thing, nevertheless. We did peek and watch what was, in fact, going on, and this is what we did in this particular case as well. And I saw quite clearly what had happened, and I heard very well what was going on. And there were blows. We counted -- somebody counted over 300 blows to Rizo Hadzalic with different things, but he didn't drop a single word. He didn't even say, "Don't, please don't." He didn't plead with them or anything of that kind. He just breathed heavily. And it was so loud and heavy that I think you could hear it, not in Omarska, but as far as Prijedor. Then they brought him and threw him down onto the pista, and he stayed alive for perhaps 20 minutes or half an hour after that. Then one of the guards came up, his name was Popovic, nicknamed Pop, and he hit him with his leg, I think for the last time, and said, "Look. This bulk is dead. This animal is dead." And that is how Rizo died. I had his jacket, which I said to myself, "If I ever survive this camp, I am going to give it to his son as a present, as a token." We will call his son Dzada. And I took that jacket with me to Trnopolje, and somebody stole it from me in Trnopolje, and I can never forgive myself for allowing it to be stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, could you identify the guards who beat Rizah Hadzalic?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As if it were today. Each of their faces. Popovic, Pop; Zeljko Savic; Drazenko Predojevic; Kricka; Zoka, Caja; and many, many others. Krkan's shift. Krkan's shift quite certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, you mentioned before an incident involving a prisoner named Hankin.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't just an incident with Hankin. It was an incident with Becir Medjunjanin. I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where did this incident take place?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why were you in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because on that day it was raining, and usually when it was raining they would take us into the canteen from the pista. But for a time they stopped doing this and then they would distribute us in the hangar building, and a group of 30 to 40 of us would be put into the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Which room in the "white house" were you put into?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second room, as you go in, on the left-hand side. When you enter the "white house," it is the second room on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What occurred while you were in that room?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were put there. In the first room there were prisoners of that infamous "white house." In that second room, I was there myself with a group of prisoners. And in the third room, or the one straight ahead when you enter the "white house," was the other half, that is, prisoners from the pista. So we were in fact divided into two groups. In the first room on the right-hand side, as you enter the house, there was a room where I recognised Eso Sadikovic, who had already come. He was a doctor; he is a well-known doctor and humanist. And some 20 minutes later, or half an hour later, two young men came into the room, Zeljko Timarac and Dusko Knezevic, nicknamed Duca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What, if anything, did they say when they came into the room?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came up to us. First of all, Dusko Knezevic spoke, nicknamed Duca, he spoke first, and he asked us whether there was anybody from Kozarac there. As there was nobody from there in that group, or in those two groups from the pista, if you like, nobody was from Kozarac, we said that there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did Duca do at that point?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He stepped back about five metres and went into the first room on the left-hand side of the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After he went into that room, what, if anything, could you hear?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Moans and groans and screams.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After some time, crawling towards our room, crawling like a dog on all fours or like a cat on all fours, his legs and arms, Becir Medjunjanin came in. Throughout that time, until he came to the door of our room, which was always open, he was beaten all the time by Dusko Knezevic, nicknamed Duca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was Timarac doing during this time?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He approached a young man called Hankin and he asked him the following: "Do you, Hankin, know anybody or any of these people who are here in this room?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did Hankin say?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he didn't know anyone and that we were all people from the surrounding villages, which wasn't true. He knew all of us very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did Timarac then do?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Timarac then proceeded to hit him with a baton, a club. On this baton there was some leather, as high as my finger [indicates] and at the top of this leather there was an iron ball. An iron ball had been attached to this piece of leather on this baton. And he hit him here [indicates] on his forehead, just once, just one blow, so that all of this was shattered. All this was shattered [indicates] and blood gushed forth. Timarac -- no, I apologise, Hankin fell down, and he continued to beat him with his hands and legs. The room is three by two metres, or three by three metres, and there were 20 of us in that room and we didn't have anywhere to flee. We would just retreat towards the wall, back towards the wall, and had we been able to, we would have broken the wall down. But as we couldn't, we all huddled up, one against the other. Then Hankin -- no, I apologise, Zeljko Timarac told us that we should all go out of the room running, and this is what we did. As we ran out of the "white house," Timarac winked at me, and I also did the same to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why do you think Timarac would have winked at you?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Timarac was a great friend of mine, a former great friend of mine. He was a football player and we used to play football together in three football teams, the teams in Prijedor; in Berek, in the OFK Prijedor, and Zitopromet, where Zeljko Timarac actually worked. He was employed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened once you left the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that we were ordered to exit in running step, we ran, and on the way, on the small path between the "white house" and the pista, when we were already on that path, we heard a shot. Most of us turned round, and I did too, and I saw Hankin next to the small steps, next to the entrance. I think there were two steps, actually, into the "white house". He was lying down on the ground, covered in blood even more, and I saw Zeljko Timarac holding a pistol in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, after you saw Hankin laying there, did you see what was done with his body?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He lay there for a time -- I don't know what happened after that -- on the grass next to the "white house." That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During the time that you saw his body on the grass next to the "white house," was he making any sounds?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was he moving in any way?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you at a distance from which you could tell whether he was breathing?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you see any signs that he was breathing?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could see, but he didn't give any signs of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in the camp after that day?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Hankin?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you know a man named (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And a man named Emir Beganovic?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were prisoners in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know, and they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you witness any incident in which they were involved?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe the incident that you saw.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. We were already in the canteen, away from the pista, and we were supposed to spend the night there. And this would usually happen about 6.00, 7.00; sometimes 5.00, sometimes 8.00, depending on the mood of the guards or the mood of the group who was on duty that day. Suddenly, from around the corner of the big hangar building, between the hangar building and the "white house," actually, (redacted), Braco Beganovic -- Emir Beganovic, nicknamed Braco, I mean, and two or three other prisoners were walking along -- I think Asaf was there, Kapetanovic -- and they were bloody. They had been beaten, they were covered in blood, and they were dirty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were the prisoners doing when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were running, fleeing. I don't know where to, but I had the impression that they were trying to flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you see who was with the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you identify that person or persons?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zigic, Dusko Knezevic, Tadic, and Janjic, a young man from Omarska who used to come specially to beat Emir Beganovic, nicknamed Braco.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You mentioned a man named Zigic. Do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you know the man before you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you know what he did for his occupation before he was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one time he worked in Croatia but then returned to work as a taxi driver in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the last thing that you saw involved in this event?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Zigic made Began drink a pool of water from the pista. You know what a pool, a puddle, is. After it was raining, there was a puddle of water there, and (redacted) had to kneel down on the pista and drink that water, and wash himself with that water too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The prisoners who were involved in these beatings and the killings that you've described, do you know what ethnic group all of those prisoners belonged to?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically all of them were Muslims. All of the ones that I enumerated and described were Muslims. There might have been a very small number of Croats who were also there and beaten. There were even a few Serbs who were beaten; and I must say that too, there were four or five Serbs in the Omarska concentration camp as well. I say that because that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, were you yourself beaten in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe the first of those incidents, please.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first of those incidents was the worst. It happened one day in July. The temperature was exceedingly hot. And we lined up, as we always did, for lunch. Suddenly, the guards came up, they were angry, and said that all of us must go outside and line up, regardless of where they were, and that nobody must remain in any of the rooms or halls that were used. So this meant that all of us had to go out to lunch. This was a bit strange because we thought, how come they were so worried whether we were going to eat or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened once you were lined up for lunch?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The groups were always groups of 30, and on the way to the entrance of the canteen, that is to say, the central building, into a short hallway, you go into a short hallway first and then turn left down the corridor and walk towards the canteen, there were 10 to 15 guards standing about in two rows, on both sides. When the prisoners passed by, or ran by -- actually, they ran -- towards lunch, they would beat them when they came to them. When they came to the canteen, they just had two to three minutes to eat their meal. Sometimes we were given five minutes, so this means they reduced the time by half. So they didn't even manage to finish their meal; they left their bread and their spoon and went to regroup in these groups of 30. They ran back the same way they had come, and once again the same thing happened, they were beaten on the way back to the pista. So those people who had lunch would be separated to one side and were not allowed to contact those who were waiting to have lunch so that they could not secretly go to the other group. So it was planned that everybody had to go to lunch, and that everybody had to be beaten on the way that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did the guards use to beat the prisoners with that day?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they covered the tiles with water; then they put trays, which were used for plates and bread, they put those down; and then some 15 to 20 centimetres above those trays, they put a sort of wire or chain -- I don't know what they used actually, wires or chains -- but the object of this whole operation was that when we rushed through there, we would slip on the tray because the tray would slip on the water, on the wet surface, and the wires and chains would do their job. So most of the prisoners in that group of 30 would fall down, one over the other, on top of the other, and then they would jump on them, stamp on them, and beat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of objects, if any, did the guards use in beating the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything they had. Batons, rifles, hands, feet, everything. They would think up all sorts of things to use to beat the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you beaten that day on your way into lunch?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And were you beaten on the way out from lunch?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I was only beaten on my back when I went into lunch. When I went out, I whispered to my colleagues, "Keep close up, one by one, and just cover your heads," because we'd already got used to being hit with clubs on our backs, so that meant nothing to us, nothing to the prisoners who had been beaten many times. But I happened to slip, and instead of going out onto the pista, I slipped and went right past, towards the corridor which led upwards to the stairway and to the interrogation room. I fell down and covered my head with my arms because I expected to be beaten, but I wasn't. And finally I exited in the normal fashion. I assumed who the guard was where I had slipped and who saved me, who didn't actually beat me then on my way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who was that guard?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guard was nicknamed Sajo. He would often watch me play as a footballer, and he told me that I got up faster than I would in a match. I was so fast that he'd never seen me get up off the grass as quickly as I did that day, when I fell down on those tiles, quicker than I'd ever done as a football player.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did the guards indicate or say anything that day which would indicate why, in your opinion, they wanted to beat everyone?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was punishment, they used to say, because several Serb soldiers from Omarska had died up at the front. I don't know where. But they were brought to Omarska to be buried there, and that was their retribution. Let me just add this because this is vitally linked to that: At that particular moment, while they were beating us, throughout that time on the stairway, on the staircase, in the window of that stairway, were the interrogators. They were there at the window, and those who interrogated us up there, they were laughing and watching it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you recognise the guards who were involved in the beating that day on the way to lunch and from lunch?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was always that same group, the experts for that kind of thing, Popovic, Savic, Kricka, Zoka, Drazenko Predojevic, and some of the guards, the special guards, whose task it was only to take us up on the upper floor for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Whose shift did those guards that you named belonged to?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krkan's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Keegan, it would be a good moment for a break. We've been working for almost an hour and a half. I should like to take advantage of the opportunity to remind you that you said you would be taking two hours with this witness, and you have already taken almost three. We will now have a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Keegan, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic --

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry. Not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you hear me now? Can you hear me? Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, but not Bosanska, only English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three. Can you hear?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps there's a problem with the B/C/S booth. No? No. Can you hear me, Witness? No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you understand English, or not? So you can't hear me. What can we do, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to deal with the problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's all right now. You may continue, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, before the break, you described --

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry, sound problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, can you hear me? Can you hear me well? Can you hear me now? Can you hear me now? Is it better now? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Keegan, let's see if you have the same connection as I and whether we can hear each other. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, before the break, you described the first of the beatings that you received.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Would you now please describe the second beating that you received.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was when the last group from the pista were moved to one of the rooms upstairs in the hangar. There were only some 30 of us. The others had already been assigned to other rooms. When we reached this last room towards the pista, we had to climb the stairs and cover the whole corridor. On the way to that corridor or to that room, rather, there were guards forming two lines. I was the first. My brother came second, and then came the others. No. Actually, my brother was number five. On the way, I just managed to tell them to cover their heads, because we had already grown accustomed to being hit on the back. They had sticks, guns, and they hit us with them. I was beaten, but not as badly as my brother and the others. His left eye was all swollen up and closed, so he couldn't see. Then the next day when we went out to the pista again, he entered Mujo's room, where Dr. Eso Sadikovic sewed up the injury using his hair, strands of hair. The night that we spent there was without a WC or anything. Guards would take out, two-by-two, sit two-by-two prisoners, I mean, and order them to fight amongst themselves while they watched.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, when you were taken into this room, and you indicated you were beaten, where were you hit?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All over my body. I protected my head like this [indicates]. I was hit on my hands but not my head, but a lot on my back. But as I have said, our backs had grown accustomed to these blows, so it wasn't as dangerous as blows on the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see the guards who were beating you and the other prisoners as you went into the room in the hangar that day?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Would you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you identify any of those guards?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only identified Soskan, because that night guards were beating who would come together with Popovic and the others, but they weren't the same people. They were the guards who were on duty in the central building, and they rarely went outside, but one of them was Soskan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you know whose shift Soskan worked on?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Krkan's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And the guards who came that evening and forced prisoners to hit each other, you identified them by name?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them was Soskan. I know the others by sight but not their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you know whose shift they were on?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same shift; Krkan's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, the third beating that you received in the camp. Where were you when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the hangar but on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that room, the largest room in the hangar, the part of it where we where was sort of surrounded by a kind of fence with pillars and a chain or wires connecting them, and on one side of that room there are three or four, maybe five toilets or WCs, and for one to go to the toilet, we had to use those toilets. To go to the toilet, you had to ask for permission, raise your hand and ask for permission. I was beaten on the way to the toilet, a couple of blows with a baton, kicks in the back, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where were you hit with the baton?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my back and head, but always -- I always protected my head with my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you recognise the guards who beat you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, but I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you know which shift those guards worked on?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know which shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And which shift was that?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milojica Kos's. His nickname is Krle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, were you ever given special treatment or extra food while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: By who?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By pupils from Maricka. I had about eight pupils who were members of the guards from Maricka, and parents -- or, rather, parents of children that I taught.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Whose shift did those former pupils or their parents work on?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Momcilo Gruban, also known as Ckalja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And on this occasion when you were given this special treatment, what did the guard do for you?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They sometimes brought me a piece of bread, and sometimes in the evening, they would take me with them into the dark to give me some food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where would they take you?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once I sat on the side of the central building, the lateral side, when you're come from Omarska and entering the camp, from the village of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where did you sit while you were out there?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a kind of wooden table and some wooden chairs, and I sat there. This was only for maybe half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: While you were out there, was anybody else out at those tables?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the next table were the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And while you were out there, were you given food?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of food were you given?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some kind of vegetables, but what I thought was most important was a piece of bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you receive any meat?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you given something to drink?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I had a glass of beer or a bottle of beer -- I can't remember -- but water I did receive, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you ever warned about danger in the camp by a guard?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And who was this guard?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was warned first by the guards who used to be my students, and I will list some of them. Zeljko Cica, Zelkjo Petos, Radovan Bozicic, Radojica Piljic, and others. And in another shift, the second shift, I was warned by a guard whose surname was Rosic. His brother went to secondary school with me and played football.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did they warn you about?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They warned me not to respond to call-outs during the night, to hide if they were not around in those shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they give you any indication of what might happen if you responded to one of these call-outs?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Liquidation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, you indicated earlier in your testimony that there were three guard shifts. Did beatings occur, beatings of prisoners occur on all three guard shifts?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did the general conditions of living in the camp that you've described, the general maltreatment, did that continue the same on all three shifts?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there any real difference between the way the three shifts acted?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, they were all the same. However, as I said yesterday, if anything can be worse than the worst, then it was the so-called Krkan's shift, Paspalj, Zoka, Popovic, Kricka, Drazenko Predojevic, Soscan, the likes of them cannot be found anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You indicated that you knew Miroslav Kvocka from before the time you were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. Not personally, but I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: While you were in the camp, were you aware of what position, if any, he held in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed, and I thought I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was that position?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant or deputy commander of the camp to Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What conduct or other indications did you have that led you to believe that he was deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the guards and the shift leaders showed respect towards him; number 2, he would bring them and distribute among them some additional food, beer, and cigarettes, especially during the night; number 3, the guard leaders would go to see him and Zeljko Meakic for consultations; and number 4, when the Serb flag would be hoisted in the morning, we usually all had to stand to attention -- believe me, we stood at attention and we had to, but the Serb soldiers would laugh and ridicule at the flag -- and every time when guard duty was being handed over, it had to be done in the presence of the shift leader or the commander or the deputy commander of the Omarska concentration camp, and this always happened at 7.00 in the morning and at 7.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see Miroslav Kvocka present at one of these shift changeovers?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you aware of what the schedule of Miroslav Kvocka's shifts were, how long his shifts were?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He and Zeljko Meakic would take turns every 24 hours, or once a day, as opposed to the shift commanders and the guards who had shifts of 12 hours each.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier in your description of the shooting of Mehmedalija Nasic that you thought that the guard Pavlic was drunk on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was it common for the guards to be drunk while they were on duty at the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, but not always. But in most cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the conduct of the guards like when they were drunk?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were even worse than when they were not drunk or when they were normal, if they were normal at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, did Miroslav Kvocka remain in this position as deputy commander at the camp for the entire time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how long Miroslav Kvocka was at the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for about a month; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Would that be a month after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you know a man named Dragoljub Prcac before you were in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. Not personally, only by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see a man by that name while you were detained in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. He took over Kvocka's role.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you say, "He took over Kvocka's role," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was deputy commander of the camp, deputy to Zeljko Meakic. He and Zeljko were the most important people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What, if any, indications or conduct did you observe that led you to believe he was the deputy commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same as in Kvocka's case; respect of guards for him, showing off. You know, they didn't hide. They were even more powerful and prouder when they marched in front of us there at the pista, with their sleeves rolled up. This is something very important. They felt even stronger and superior to us. They carried pump-action guns and weapons that differed from the weapons of the guards. Therefore, it was no secret, and they themselves, the guards, talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, when you said, "They were even more powerful and prouder when they marched in front of us there at the pista," who are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the camp commanders: Meakic, Kvocka, Prcac. And the others too, the investigators, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You referred to them as carrying pump-action guns, Pumperica. Who carried such a gun in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dragoljub Prcac carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of weapon did he have?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A pistol and automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you ever recall an occasion where Dragoljub Prcac was calling out prisoners while you were present?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Oklopcic, I'd like you at this time to please look around the courtroom and indicate whether or not you can identify the individual that you've described as Miroslav Kvocka. If you can do so, please point him out and describe him.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last row, between Radic and Milojica Kos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could please describe the colour of suit and the colour of shirt that he is wearing.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His shirt is blue, and whether the suit is blue or dark, in any case, I think it's blue, as far as I can see from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
