utterances.text: Just to make sure we can be clear, since you haven't identified the other individuals you've named yet, counting from the door, the entrance door there, and moving to the right, counting the persons, which number is he, from the door to the right?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To make myself clear, the first man is Radic, called Krkan; the second is Kvocka, Miroslav; and the third -- if you wish me to continue, I can give you all of them, no problem there, because we know each other very well, it's just our roles have changed -- but Kvocka has a little -- I have a slight, slight respect for him because he managed to save three Muslim lives, and that means something out of these thousands of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who is the third individual in that back row? You didn't mention his name.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milojica Kos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And the individual --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Shena Milojica. "Shena Milojica," the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you see the individual who you've described as Dragoljub Prcac present?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, yes. Left from Zigic, between the policeman and Zigic, in the first row.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And then the second individual in the first row is?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wearing a red suit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Zigic. Zigic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is that the man you indicated you saw in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I would like to offer into evidence first the map that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, do you have an objection to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, only with regard to the transcript. It says that the witness said "Senna Milojica."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said Milojica Kos.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there's the word "Senna". It says "Senna" here, and I don't know what "Senna" means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, maybe it's a mistake of some kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've already said that the court reporters revise the transcript at least three times, go through it at least three times, so you're going to receive a written transcript. There is always a deadline, and you can make corrections. But at any rate, we can correct that straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Let me say that that word does not mean anything in our language. "Senna" means the Seine, the river, in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Yes, words always mean something to some of us. So as you know, there is the connotation of the word, or the meaning of a word. But at any rate, thank you for drawing our attention to that, Mr. Fila, and I think that we have regulated that matter, or it will be regulated. I think that Mr. Keegan hadn't completed yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I could just beg your indulgence a few minutes longer. I was mindful of your reminder earlier about the time, but there are a couple of documents that I would like to offer into evidence, which should take only a couple of minutes for the witness to authenticate and describe. As well as the map which was used yesterday, that area map of Prijedor, which was Exhibit 1/26, I'd also like to offer at this time. If this first document could be shown, it would be marked as Exhibit 3/76. Copies have already been provided, both in B/C/S and English, to the Defence. I'm reminded that this would be 3/78, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are there any objections on the part of the Defence with respect to these documents being tendered? I see that somebody was shaking their head. Mr. Simic, would you tell us whether there are any objections or not, for the purposes of the record? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. So we admit these documents into evidence, Mr. Keegan. Does that complete your examination-in-chief, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'd like to at least have the witness describe what the import of the document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now see that Exhibit 3/78 was not presented, shown, to the witness, 3/78, was it, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, it was not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So perhaps we should have the witness declare himself with respect to this document. I see it is a document with personal data.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document, it says that this is a certificate, the first document, that I was in the Trnopolje camp from the 3rd of August, 1989, and that I was released -- I mean 1992, I beg your pardon, I made a mistake -- it is not 1989, it is 1992 -- and that I was released on the 14th of August, 1992. First of all, there's a mistake there, because I came from the Omarska camp on the 5th, the last group of us 70 people to be singled out. And a day later, as far as we heard, this camp was dismantled and some of the prisoners went to Manjaca and some went to Trnopolje. This document was signed by an interpreter in the Red Cross, Pero Curguz, and Slobodan Kuruzovic, the commander of the Trnopolje camp. The second document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You haven't been shown that yet. The second document would be 3 --

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there's a mistake here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The second document, that would be the English translation of it. It would be Exhibit 3/79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you finished, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As soon as the witness has had an opportunity to describe the document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: AZEDIN OKLOPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second document, I spent 11 -- no, nine days in Trnopolje, and during that time, a certain number of prisoners were allowed to go home. Any friend, a Serb soldier, could come to take you out, and ask Slobodan Kuruzovic to let you to go home, get permission for you to go home. First of all, my kum, who was a Serb, came, but he didn't succeed to take me out. Then the director of my school, Captain First Class, he didn't succeed either. After that, a policeman, my friend and a regular policeman -- I don't want to name people, I'm not going to name him -- he didn't succeed either. Slobodan Kuruzovic was my teacher and my director of the school when I worked there temporarily from time to time or when I was a replacement of teachers in the 16th of May School. When I asked him, who was a great friend of my mother and father, former great friend, "Why can everybody go home and I can't, Slobodan?" I asked him, and he said, "No. You have to put on a little weight so that your mother can recognise you when you come home." And as there were some killings in Trnopolje, I was a little surprised at this. And I persuaded my wife to go to the SUP in Prijedor and to ask for a decision, a certificate of this kind, a decision whereby permitting me -- it says, "Oklopcic, Huse Mirela," and that is my wife's name, Mirela, she was born on such-and-such a day, and the address is Prijedor, Rade Koncar 3, and to allow her to leave the autonomous Province of Krajina, and the explanation for this was that she tabled a request on the 10th of August. I don't want the dates to mislead you, but this is the time when I was actually in the camp. And the decision was issued on the 19th of August, when I had left the camp. However, on the 10th of August, or one or two days after that date, after sending in the request and paying a tax that had to be paid to the SUP in Prijedor, she brought me a certificate saying that she had tendered this request and that she had paid the tax necessary, and on the basis of that certificate I was able to leave the Trnopolje concentration camp and go home. But the original -- the original document, it was received by us on the 19th of August, that is to say, five days after I had left the concentration camp of Trnopolje, and that is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That concludes my examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to repeat my question. Are there any objections from the Defence with respect to these documents, these exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. We object to the admission of document 3/78. The witness informed the Court that he was unable to authenticate the document. It contains incorrect information. Therefore, in my submission, it's inadmissible. As for document 3/79 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can -- we're making legal submission, Your Honour. It may be inappropriate for the witness to be listening, and, I submit, inappropriate for him to comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a mistake. I apologise. I must say that that is a mistake. I didn't say that. The document, could you clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for a moment. I'm going to ask you one more time. Mr. O'Sullivan, have you completed what you are going to say or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still have this doubt as to whether you understand English or not, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you take off your headset for a moment, please, if you will. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have made my objection to the admissibility of document 3/78. In regards to document 3/79, again, in my submission, the witness has failed to authenticate that document. Therefore, it is an unreliable document which should not be admitted into evidence. Those are my submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness testified that the first document, 3/78, was a document that he obtained in order to be -- indicate his detention in the camp, and the second one was a document which his wife obtained for them to be able to leave the area. Now, again, I'm happy to go through the basic foundation questions such as to ask him does he have the originals of these two documents and is that how these copies were prepared, and I can continue through those kind of foundational questions if the Court finds it necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you have the original documents? Yes. Please put your headset on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean this document here? Is this the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is -- I don't know whether you have the number, but it is a two-page document, yes. That's right. That's the one, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should like to ask the gentleman to repeat once again, because I now have the interpretation, what he is not clear on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Please answer me, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It has my particulars here, my birth, the number of my identity card, my place and birth, and where I come from. And here is the date of reception, the 3rd of August, 1992. Gentlemen, I did not write this piece of paper myself, it was written by Pero Curguz and Slobodan Kuruzovic. And in Trnopolje, I arrived on the 5th of August, when the concentration camp in Keraterm was dismantled. And we were the last group of 70 people to arrive on this particular day, and the concentration camp from Trnopolje. Later on, one day later, 1.000 prisoners from Omarska came for Trnopolje on the 6th and the other half went to Manjaca, which means that this document, I did not sign it. For the purposes of truth, I state that I came to the Trnopolje on the 5th of August and not the 3rd of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, we have here in the Tribunal a sui generis proceeding, and I don't want to compare the system of common law and civil law. We have our own system here at the Tribunal, and you know full well that in the common-law system, the question of admissibility is the priority issue, because finally all the proof and evidence must be reviewed by the Judges to be presented to the jury. We do not have -- this is not a trial by jury. The Judges here are professional Judges, and it is possible, in keeping with our rules and regulations, to present all the proof and evidence that the Judges and the Trial Chamber wish to have and to have admitted, and later on, it is up to the Judges to give it the probative value that they see fit. So the rules and regulations allow the Trial Chamber to admit documents, and this Trial Chamber will be admitting these documents, and they will be a part of the file. Now I would like to turn to Mr. Simic, Mr. Krstan Simic, to know the order of the cross-examination. Who is going to start? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have had some problems with the Prosecution, and Mr. O'Sullivan will explain the nature of the problems that have cropped up, and the results of that negotiation will be expounded to the members of the Prosecution. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, following on from what Mr. Simic has just said, it will be Mr. O'Sullivan who is going to take the floor, and I do give the floor to Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: This morning we've had a meeting prior to the hearing, prior to the beginning of the hearing, with the Prosecution, in fact, all Defence counsel and the Prosecution, and my understanding, at the conclusion of that meeting, is that Ms. Hollis was going to address the Chamber following the examination-in-chief of this witness. I believe Ms. Hollis would like to speak with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Madam Hollis, would you like to have this discussion in the presence of the witness, or would you like the witness to go out, or is it sufficient for him to remove his headset?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would ask that the witness be excused, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, we apologise, but we should like to ask you to step outside the courtroom for a minute, and this will give you an extra chance for a break and have a rest, and after that we shall call you back in again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as Defence counsel Mr. O'Sullivan indicated, we did have a meeting with the Defence this morning. That followed a written notice to the Defence that was put in their lockers last night. The situation, to be very candid and straightforward is this, Your Honours: The Prosecution has failed to make timely and complete disclosure of material relevant to several witnesses who are next in order on the witness list submitted on the 28th of April. As I indicated, we gave written notice to Defence counsel last night. We gave oral notice to them this morning. We have begun to make disclosure but that is not complete. Previously, the Prosecution had instituted a procedure to review the disclosure that had been made in this case to identify materials that had not been disclosed and to provide disclosure. This trial team failed to provide disclosure of materials which had been identified. Certainly this failure was not malicious, but, nonetheless, the trial team failed to discharge our obligations in a timely and complete fashion. As a result of this, Defence counsel has indicated to us that they are not prepared to continue with the cross-examination of this witness, nor are they prepared to continue beyond the direct-examination of this witness. They indicated they are prepared to continue with witnesses beginning on Monday, the 15th of May. Your Honours, the Prosecution certainly understands the full significance of our failure to make proper disclosure. We offer our apologies to the Court, to the counsel, and to the accused. We do not offer excuses because we have no excuse. It was a failure within the team. As I said, we are taking steps even now to correct it, but, nonetheless, because of our failure, we find ourselves in our current circumstances, and I wish to give this very straightforward and candid explanation to the Court before the Defence makes any further submissions they may wish to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis, you mentioned measures which you have in mind to remedy the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour. Of course, the very first measure that we must take and that we're undertaking at this moment is to provide the disclosure that we should have provided. We have provided some of that disclosure in both languages but not in a timely fashion. In other instances, we have provided the disclosure in English but not in B/C/S, and in some instances, we are at present unable to provide the disclosure in either language because it is in a third language that needs translation. The material that has not been disclosed because of translation has been submitted for translation with an explanation of the urgency of the request. Other materials which are not statements have been provided so that copies can be made and they can be distributed to the Defence as soon as possible. Those are the measures that we have undertaken to accomplish this disclosure. Now, in terms of the other remedies that might be available, we asked the Defence this morning if they were willing to allow to us proceed, to conclude this direct-examination, and they very graciously indicated they were willing to allow this direct-examination to conclude. They indicated, as to additional witnesses, however, they would not be prepared to proceed until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Hollis. You mentioned that the Defence allowed you graciously to continue the direct-examination only of this witness or of the other witnesses too, and then they can cross-examine when they have the documents? What was their gracious reply?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: They specifically indicated that they would allow us to complete the direct-examination of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Only this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We asked if they would be prepared to proceed with the other witnesses. They indicated no. As to whether they would allow direct examination to continue, I did not ask that specific question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That is the examination with the other witnesses. Did they say no?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I did not ask that specific question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, just so I understand, last week when we had our few days of discussion about the procedures that would be followed in the trial, was it evident then to you or to the Defence counsel that this disclosure had not been completed?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am the senior trial attorney who has carriage of this case, and I regret to inform you that at that time it was not evident to me. It was my understanding that identified material had been disclosed. My understanding was in error, and I accept responsibility for that. I learned this weekend that information as to one witness had not been disclosed. We made efforts and disclosed that this weekend, but it was not timely, of course. Yesterday, I learned that the other material had not been disclosed, and yesterday and last night and this morning we have taken steps to remedy that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So we could be assured that if the witnesses were heard beginning next week that the necessary disclosure would have been completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to the extent that it is an issue of English to B/C/S, yes. We have some languages -- some statements in a language not of this Tribunal, not an official language. We would certainly make all efforts to ensure that would happen. Those are not -- let me check my list, Your Honour. That would involve two statements of a witness who is number 8 on the list, so that the other witnesses before them, we should be prepared for that, Your Honour. As I said, we had previously identified materials, and where the procedure went off the track was then taking the least difficult of all steps, and that was to provide the disclosure of the identified materials, and we are taking steps at this point to correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Last question: So until you discovered the error in your own procedures, it would not have been possible for the Defence to know that they were not getting everything?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it would not have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis, in order to be able to understand the overall situation, I would like to ask you the following: In relation to the disclosure, Rule 66, how can this have happened? I don't know if you've quite understood my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I exactly understand your question, and I myself do not know how it happened, but I do know that it did happen. I also know that when I became involved in the case, one of the first things I asked for was that a comprehensive search be conducted so that we could determine if we had met our obligations. As that search was conducted, then I asked a review be made so that items could be identified that had not been disclosed, so that then we could provide disclosure. So this system was begun some time ago. It should have been begun much earlier. I personally have no understanding as to why that did not happen, but, at any rate, it was begun some time ago. We took it in order of witnesses to be sure we would be able to provide prompt disclosure upon identifying material that was not disclosed. That material was, in fact, identified. The disclosures that should have been made were not made because of internal problems within the team. Again, as senior trial attorney, I accept responsibility for that. When I became aware of the particular items that indeed had not been disclosed, contrary to my understanding, then we began to take immediate steps to correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Hollis. We understand that your personal situation is that you replaced Mr. Niemann, and, therefore, we understand that this can occur when there is a change in the team, but there is something that the Chamber regrets, and that is the Prosecutor has always said that it is ready to begin trial, and we're always having problems. There is at least one thing, and I think I speak on behalf of all my colleagues, something that concerns us very much, and that is the position of witnesses. Last week we have five witnesses, and we had the problems we had. Now we have I don't know how many witnesses. Perhaps it is not a relevant question, but it is relevant, the fact that these witnesses are waiting. And when we think about remedies, and that was the gist of my question and the question put by my colleague Judge Riad, I would like at least to consider the hypothesis of the examination-in-chief of the witnesses who are here, because that would help us to make progress with the case, if the Defence agrees. The Defence will have time to prepare. We could hear the testimony of witnesses who are present. Otherwise, the witnesses will be waiting, without doing nothing. On the other hand, we could have the examination. It's true that the witnesses could have more days here, more time spent here, but I think this would be a possibility of dealing with this. Because the very idea of suspending the hearings and postponing them, I think we have to take advantage of the resources which the International Community has put at our disposal, we must use them well economically, and that is why I'm asking this question. Madam Hollis, I'm addressing you now, and afterwards the Defence: Could we hear the witnesses who are here present only for their examination-in-chief, and after that the witnesses could come back for the cross-examination, after having given the Defence the necessary time to prepare. That is my question and suggestion, Madam Hollis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Certainly, Your Honour, the Prosecution is prepared to go forward with direct on all these witnesses. We would point out, not on behalf of the Prosecution, but another consideration for Your Honours, and that is, if the witnesses do testify on direct and then some time passes before they are cross-examined, there is the issue about whether they would be, in some way, secluded, or how restrictive any communications they may have would be in order to prevent any type of influence or change of testimony. So there is a concern that once they begin their testimony, perhaps they should do it in toto. We weren't able to prevent that situation with Mr. Oklopcic. But with the other witnesses, perhaps it would be better for the witnesses if they didn't have those kinds of restraints on the contact they can have. Because once they give their direct, of course, they are under oath, they have given their direct, but they've not yet been subjected to cross-examination, so the kind of communication they may have with other people, the kind of interaction they may have with other people, may be very restricted. Again, that is simply a concern we would raise for Your Honours to consider. But in terms of being prepared to go forward with the direct, the Prosecution is prepared to go forward with the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor now to the Defence. I don't know if there is a spokesman. I see Mr. O'Sullivan rising. I think we have two questions to consider: First, the possibility of having the direct of witnesses, and to possibly make an exception to the decision of the Chamber regarding communication by witnesses after the taking of the oath. Of course, this would apply also to Defence witnesses should the same circumstances occur. Could you give us your opinion and assist us, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First, on behalf of the defendants, let me say that we very much appreciate the candor and graciousness of Ms. Hollis, who finds herself in a very difficult, if not embarrassing, situation, and we have sympathy for that. We do, however, oppose calling the next witness. Your Honour, the disclosure provisions of the Rules exist for a reason, and for one very important reason, and that is so that the defendants have adequate time to prepare to meet the case against them. Ms. Hollis has not gone over the list of shortcomings in disclosure, and I wouldn't expect her to in court, but she did with us this morning, and I think it's fair to say that there are a number of items which have not been disclosed and which we need before testimony can continue. That is our position. I think Ms. Hollis has made a strong submission that this is a problem, it's a problem for the Defence for us to continue, and that is why we joined Ms. Hollis in asking for an adjournment until Monday, with the proviso, of course, that the Prosecution can in fact disclose to us those materials which are going to be relevant at least for the witnesses next week. Now, we said a reasonable delay and a necessary delay was until next Monday, but that was on the assumption that we get at least those documents for those first few witnesses who are next. So an adjournment is necessary, it's required for us to be ready, with the proviso that those important documents for the next witnesses are provided to us. If I can be of any further assistance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. O'Sullivan. I'm fully aware of the necessity of the adjournment for the cross-examination, but what is the necessity for the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It's an issue of being prepared for these witnesses, to see what their statements say, to see what other documentation is relevant to what they will testify to, which is the whole basis and reason for disclosure under Rule 66, so that we know what's coming. As it stands now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Don't you have enough time to know it before the cross-examination, which would be, really, your role?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In my submission, we must know that before the witness comes into court, before that witness testifies. That is the essence and the heart of Rule 66 and the reason for it being there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I just wanted to make it clear for the record, based on your comments that perhaps because I come from a military background, but I do not want any of my comments to be interpreted as an attempt to excuse myself from responsibility because of my involvement in the case. When I said, as the senior trial attorney I take responsibility for this, that is what I meant. So I wasn't trying to excuse my failure to correct this situation, and I just wanted that to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Hollis, we understand that, but we find ourselves in a very difficult situation, as you well understand. There are organisational problems, which I attribute mostly to the change in the team. But the Prosecution has put us in a difficult situation, that is the truth, and we are not here to judge you. On the contrary. We appreciate very much, as has already been said by Mr. O'Sullivan, your frankness and your honesty, but that does not remove the problem. I think the best thing to do would be to have a 30-minute break, and then we are going to come here with a decision as to what we are going to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. The Chamber is of the opinion that, in the face of this situation, the rights of the accused and the Defence would be prejudiced slightly if we were to order the continuation of work. It should be remembered that the framework for the conduct of proceedings is provided by two main lines: It has to be fair and expeditious. We cannot, in the interest of efficiency, fail in terms of fairness. But as we have always said, the Chamber conducts its work in an explanatory manner, which means that this adjournment is going to cost the Prosecution three days envisaged for the presentation of its case. That is a decision, if one could use the Latin phrase, bonus pater familias. Therefore, the Chamber is going to suspend the hearing until Monday, and asks the Prosecutor to do everything in its power to make up for the time lost in the presentation of the case. The Chamber also notes the good cooperation between the parties, which should be maintained in the future to truly speed up and conclude this trial within the framework of fairness and expeditiousness. We have a great deal of work to do, the parties and the Judges, so we're going to meet here again next Monday, at 9.30, and the Chamber hopes that we will really be ready to resume the trial then. That is the decision of the Chamber.
